meta.ogDescription: Not Lincoln. An old anonymous law adage, in print by 1795 and called an Italian proverb — Quote Investigator traces it well before Lincoln.

answer.label: Not Abraham Lincoln — an anonymous legal proverb
answer.authorDates: In print by 1795 · described then as an Italian proverb
answer.sourceLine: This is a proverb of unknown authorship, not a Lincoln original. A partial match appears as early as 1682 (“he who will be his own Counsellour, shall be sure to have a Fool for his Client”), and the lawyer-specific wording is in print by 1795, where Quote Investigator ↗ notes it was credited to an Italian proverb. The attribution to Abraham Lincoln is late and undocumented.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: It is an old law adage, copied from the Italian proverb … that the man who is his own lawyer has a fool for his client.
trail: A partial match — “he who will be his own Counsellour, shall be sure to have a Fool for his Client” — appears in William De Britaine’s Humane Prudence (1682), per Quote Investigator ↗.
The lawyer-specific wording is in print by 1795 in The British Critic, which frames it as an old law adage “copied from the Italian proverb,” per Quote Investigator ↗.
Henry Kett’s The Flowers of Wit (1814) prints “every man who is his own lawyer, has a fool for a client,” the earliest example cited by phrases.org.uk ↗.
Quote Investigator ↗ concludes the saying is anonymous and circulated before Lincoln’s birth in 1809; a popular Lincoln credit surfaces only much later (e.g., a 1966 Bewitched episode).
source.excerptNote: As printed in The British Critic (1795), per Quote Investigator ↗. Wordings vary (“his client” / “a client”) across the 18th–19th-century sources.

source.rightsNote: This is an anonymous proverb with no identifiable author or single originating work — its lawyer-specific wording was already circulating in print by 1795. Because no fixed authored source underlies the line, no copyright status can be asserted; the early printed texts that carry it (1682–1815) are long in the public domain, but the proverb itself is not a copyrightable authored work.

author.name: Anonymous — an old legal proverb
author.heading: About Anonymous — an old legal proverb
author.metaLine: In print by 1795 · English/Italian legal proverb · popularly mis-credited to Lincoln
author.bio: This adage belongs to the anonymous proverb tradition, not to any single author. Its earliest known lawyer-specific printing (1795, The British Critic) explicitly calls it an Italian proverb, and partial forms about being “one’s own counsellor” go back to William De Britaine’s Humane Prudence (1682). Abraham Lincoln, a practicing lawyer, may well have repeated it, but he did not originate it and no contemporary record documents him saying this exact line.

misattribution.heading: Why Lincoln gets the credit — and why it's wrong
misattribution.intro: The line is routinely pinned on Abraham Lincoln, a famous frontier lawyer, which makes the attribution feel plausible. But the proverb was already in print decades before Lincoln was born.

items.why: No documented speech, letter, or contemporary account has Lincoln coining or uttering this exact line. Quote Investigator ↗ finds the Lincoln credit is late and unsupported; a widely-seen instance is a 1966 Bewitched episode that attributes it to him.

items.who: An anonymous law adage / Italian proverb
items.why: The lawyer-specific wording appears in The British Critic in 1795 as “an old law adage, copied from the Italian proverb,” with partial forms back to 1682 — well before Lincoln (b. 1809), per Quote Investigator ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: It’s an anonymous legal proverb in print by 1795 — not a Lincoln original, per Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: An adage older than the man it's credited to
lead: The saying warns that anyone who represents himself in a legal dispute lacks the detachment a real advocate would bring — his “client” is poorly served because his “lawyer” is himself. It is one of a family of parallel proverbs, including “he who is his own doctor has a fool for a patient.”

Because Lincoln was the era’s most famous self-taught lawyer, the proverb migrated onto him in the 20th century — a textbook case of a floating aphorism attaching to a magnetic name long after the words themselves were coined.
context.pull: In print by 1795, and called an Italian proverb even then.
